learningObjective: Precisely define a basic block and identify what constitutes a valid CFG edge.

canonicalClaims.claim: A basic block is a maximal straight-line sequence of instructions with exactly one entry point and one exit point; the CFG has a directed edge from BB_i to BB_j when control can transfer from the terminator of BB_i to the entry of BB_j.
conditions: Instructions inside a block are executed in sequence from entry to exit without intra-block branches.
Exceptions and calls may or may not be treated as terminators depending on the analysis's precision needs.
nonImplications: Does not imply BBs cannot contain function calls.
Does not imply the maximal-BB partition is the only valid partitioning; smaller BB granularities are allowed.

misconceptions.claim: Basic blocks group instructions that are data-independent.
misconceptions.whyWrong: BBs are defined by control-flow entry/exit properties, not by data dependency.

misconceptions.claim: A basic block equals a function body.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Functions typically contain many BBs; call graphs (which have a node per function) are different from CFGs.

misconceptions.claim: A basic block equals a loop body.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Loops are structural features of the CFG; they typically contain multiple BBs including a header, latch, and body blocks.

implementationFacts: In LLVM, each BB is a llvm::BasicBlock terminated by a terminator instruction (br, ret, switch, invoke, etc.).
Fall-through edges are made explicit in LLVM by an unconditional br to the successor block.
performanceScenarios: Optimization passes operate on BBs (e.g., local CSE) or across BBs guided by the CFG (e.g., global DCE).
